dct_creator_sm: Subarctic Lakes in a Changing Climate (SLACC) Lab, Aurora Research Institute (ARI ).
dct_description_sm:
Between 1948 and 1999, gold mining activities in the Yellowknife area generated large amounts of arsenic contamination, leaving an environmental legacy on the landscape. This study sampled 98 lakes within 30 km of the City of Yellowknife to document surface water quality and mining impacts in an area exposed to 50 years of emissions from gold ore processing. 

Sampling occurred in September 2012 and 2014 from a helicopter equipped with floats. Field measurements were recorded for specific conductivity, pH, dissolved oxygen, total dissolved solids, and water temperature, while surface grab samples were taken for lab analysis. These samples were analyzed for major ions, cations, nutrients, physicals, and dissolved metals.

Concentrations of arsenic, antimony, and sulphate were elevated in lakes within 17.5 km of Giant Mine relative to lakes beyond this distance. Arsenic concentrations were highest in small lakes (<100 ha) that were downwind and proximal to the historic stacks, suggesting a gradient in impact from historic roaster operations at Giant Mine consistent with the predominant wind direction in the region. Concentrations of arsenic exceeded the federal drinking water guideline of 10 µg/L for many of the lakes sampled within 12 km of the roaster stacks, and in some lakes were more than 60 times this limit. 

This study provides an extensive survey of elemental concentrations in regional lakes surrounding the City of Yellowknife and should be supported by future work to investigate drivers of variation in arsenic concentration in surface waters, interannual variability in water chemistry, and the long-term fate of arsenic and other elements of potential concern in these lakes.

dct_title_s: The concentration of arsenic in lake waters of the Yellowknife area
